title: Identity paths derived from truncated key fingerprints (32-bit GPG short ID, 64-bit DID hash)
description:
EXPLOITABLE with keyring/env write access; the GPG case is cheap enough to be practical today.

Two locations, same pattern - a truncated fingerprint used as the identity component of a SPIFFE ID:

1. persona-attestors/src/gpg.rs:80-85, make_claim():
       let short_fp = fingerprint[fingerprint.len() - 8..].to_lowercase();
       SpiffeId::new(TrustDomain::SshLocal, format!("gpg/{short_fp}"))
   The last 8 hex characters of an OpenPGP fingerprint is the 32-bit "short key ID". Short key IDs are collidable in seconds on commodity hardware - this is the 2016 Evil32 result, which precomputed colliding short IDs for the entire PGP strong set. An attacker who can add a key to the users keyring (gpg.rs reads ~/.gnupg via gpg --list-keys) generates a key whose short ID matches a trusted key and receives the identical SPIFFE ID spiffe://ssh.local/gpg/<shortid>.

2. persona-attestors/src/did_key.rs:36-39, did_short_id():
       let hash = Sha256::digest(did.as_bytes());
       hash[..8]...                       // 64 bits
       SpiffeId::new(TrustDomain::SshLocal, format!("did/{short}"))  // did_key.rs:70
   64 bits gives a birthday collision around 2^32 work and a targeted second preimage around 2^64. The first is trivial; the second is expensive but not out of reach, and there is no reason to truncate at all here.

CONSEQUENCE: the SPIFFE ID is the authorization subject. Two distinct keys mapping to one SPIFFE ID means a relying partys allow-list entry for a legitimate key also authorizes the attackers colliding key, and audit logs cannot tell the two apart. Truncation buys nothing - the full 40-hex fingerprint / full SHA-256 hex is a legal SPIFFE path segment.

Fix direction: use the full fingerprint (GPG) and the full 32-byte hash hex or the did:key multibase value itself (DID). If a short display form is wanted, keep it in display_name, not in the identity path.
